memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "Say to them: 'Any Israelite or any foreigner residing among them who offers a burnt offering or sacrifice and does not bring it to the entrance to the tent of meeting to sacrifice it to the LORD must be cut off from the people of Israel.'" - Lev 17:8-9 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Any Israelite or any foreigner residing among them. That phrase appears repeatedly in this chapter, and it is easy to skim past.

Foreigners lived among Israel — traders, servants, people who had attached themselves to this nation and its God. And God does not write them a separate rulebook. The same standard, the same access, the same accountability.

That was unusual. Ancient religions were generally tribal. Your gods belonged to your people, and outsiders had no real standing.

But Israel's God had said to Abraham at the very beginning that all peoples on earth would be blessed through him (Gen 12:3). Rahab of Jericho and Ruth of Moab both ended up in the family line of Jesus. Isaiah looked ahead to a house of prayer for all nations (Isa 56:7).

And then Peter, standing in a Gentile's house, said the words that changed the shape of the church: I now realise how true it is that God does not show favouritism but accepts from every nation the one who fears him (Acts 10:34-35).

If you have ever felt like an outsider to God's people — wrong background, wrong history, arriving late — read this verse again. The same rule. The same welcome.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Have you ever felt like an outsider among God's people?
2. Does your church genuinely welcome those who do not fit the usual mould?
3. What does God's inclusion of the foreigner tell you about His heart?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, thank You that Your welcome has always reached beyond one nation and one background. Make me someone who welcomes others as freely as You have welcomed me. Amen.
